title: A Great Multitude No One Could Number
theme: Before the winds of judgment are released, God seals his servants, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a countless multitude from every nation standing before the throne in white robes, having come out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the Lamb's blood, now sheltered and shepherded by God forever.

language.gloss: to seal, mark as one's own
language.note: A seal on the forehead marks God's ownership and protection. It answers the question of 6:17: God's sealed people can stand. Elsewhere the New Testament says believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30), and in Revelation the mark is the name of the Lamb and his Father (14:1).

A 'great multitude that no one could number,' from every nation, tribe, people and language. The number of the redeemed recalls God's promise that Abraham's offspring would be as countless as the stars (Genesis 15:5).

With the article in Greek, 'the great tribulation.' Some take it as a specific future period; others as the whole time of suffering for God's people, which John already shares (1:9). Either way, the multitude has 'come out of' it victorious.

language.gloss: to tabernacle, spread a tent over
language.note: God 'will spread his tent over them' (ESV 'shelter them with his presence'). The word recalls the tabernacle and the glory cloud over Israel, and John's Gospel uses it of the Word who 'dwelt among us' (John 1:14). It is fulfilled in 21:3.
The Lamb becomes the Shepherd. The Lamb who was led to slaughter now leads his flock to springs of living water, fulfilling Psalm 23 and Isaiah 49.

usage.theme: A mark of protection before judgment
usage.note: Blood on the doorposts at Passover and the mark on the foreheads in Ezekiel set apart God's faithful before judgment fell.
God's promise of a numberless family to Abraham is fulfilled in a multitude from every nation who belong to Christ.
The redeemed take no credit; salvation is God's work from beginning to end.
Isaiah's promise that God will swallow up death and wipe away tears from all faces appears here and again at the end of the book.

context.setting: Chapter 7 is an interlude between the sixth and seventh seals. The sixth seal ended with the question, 'Who shall be able to stand?' (6:17), and chapter 7 answers it with two visions of God's people: sealed on earth before judgment, and standing victorious in heaven after it. A similar interlude comes between the sixth and seventh trumpets (10:1-11:14). The identity of the 144,000 is one of the most debated questions in the book.

flow.label: The winds held back
flow.note: Four angels restrain the winds of judgment until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads.

flow.label: The 144,000
flow.note: John hears the number sealed: 12,000 from each of twelve tribes of Israel.

flow.label: The great multitude
flow.note: John sees a countless multitude from every nation in white robes with palm branches, crying 'Salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb,' and all the angels worship.

flow.label: Who they are
flow.note: An elder explains: they came out of the great tribulation, washed their robes in the Lamb's blood, and now serve God, who shelters them; the Lamb shepherds them and God wipes away every tear.

tier1.note: 'They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun smite them: for he that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water.' John quotes Isaiah almost word for word.
'The Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces.'
A mark set on the foreheads of those who grieved over the city's sin, sparing them from the judgment that followed.

tier2.note: God promised Abraham descendants beyond counting; the multitude fulfills it.
The LORD my shepherd leads me beside still waters. The Lamb now shepherds his people.
'A time of trouble, such as never was,' when God's people are delivered. Jesus uses this language for great tribulation (Matthew 24:21).
Palm branches and dwelling in booths marked the Feast of Tabernacles, a joyful harvest festival. The multitude celebrates under God's 'tent.'

tier3.note: The Passover blood marked Israel's houses so the destroyer passed over.
Jesus is both the Lamb of God who takes away sin and the good shepherd who lays down his life.
Paul speaks of true Jewishness as a matter of the heart and calls the church 'the Israel of God,' texts often used in the debate about the 144,000.

voices.name: Richard Bauckham
voices.work: The Climax of Prophecy: Studies on the Book of Revelation
voices.view: Bauckham argues that the 144,000 John hears and the multitude he sees are the same group, just as he heard of a Lion and saw a Lamb (5:5-6). The 144,000 present God's people as the messianic army of Israel; the multitude reveals that this army is drawn from every nation and conquers through the Lamb's blood.

voices.name: John MacArthur
voices.view: MacArthur takes the 144,000 as literal ethnic Jews, 12,000 from each tribe, who will be saved and protected during the future tribulation and serve as evangelists. He takes the multitude as people saved during that period through their witness.

voices.name: G. K. Beale
voices.work: The Book of Revelation (New International Greek Testament Commentary)
voices.view: Beale sees the 144,000 as a symbolic number for the complete people of God, Jew and Gentile, pictured as the true Israel. The number is twelve (tribes) times twelve (apostles) times a thousand, an image of completeness and fullness.

translations.kjv: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

renderings.text: These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation
they who have come out of the great tribulation
the ones who come out of the great tribulation

translations.note: The Greek has the article, 'the great tribulation,' which the KJV omits. It also uses a present participle, 'the ones coming out,' which ESV keeps. That may picture a continuing stream of believers coming through tribulation over time.

steps.gospel: The answer to 'who shall be able to stand?' is all who belong to the Lamb. They stand not because they were strong but because they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (v14), a paradox only the cross explains. They cry, 'Salvation belongs to our God,' taking no credit. And the final picture is of the Lamb as Shepherd: no more hunger, thirst or scorching heat, living water, and God himself wiping away every tear. The promise to Abraham of a numberless family from every nation is kept in Christ.
application: Take comfort that God marks and keeps his people before judgment falls. You belong to him.
Rejoice in the global church. Heaven's worship is multinational and multilingual.
Do not expect to escape all tribulation. The multitude came out of it, not around it, and it did not have the last word.
Give all credit for your salvation to God and the Lamb.
Hold onto the promise of verse 17 in grief. God himself will wipe away every tear.

misapplications.claim: Only 144,000 people will go to heaven or reign with Christ.
misapplications.correction: Immediately after hearing the 144,000, John sees a multitude 'which no man could number' before the throne (v9). Whatever view one takes of the 144,000, heaven is not limited to them.

misapplications.claim: Being washed in the blood means our own suffering makes us clean.
misapplications.correction: The robes are made white 'in the blood of the Lamb' (v14). Christ's sacrifice, not our endurance, cleanses; endurance is the fruit of belonging to him.

misapplications.claim: The list of tribes is a precise prediction that can be used to identify modern tribal descendants.
misapplications.correction: The list is unusual: Dan is missing, and Joseph and Manasseh both appear while Ephraim does not. Its arrangement seems to carry symbolic meaning; it is not a genealogical guide.

contrasts.note: Many see these as two views of the same people; others as two groups.
Those who came out of great suffering are now covered by God's own presence.
Every deprivation of the wilderness is reversed.
The sacrificial victim becomes the one who guides and protects.

features.label: An interlude that answers
features.note: Chapter 7 interrupts the seals to answer 6:17. Revelation regularly pauses its judgments to show where God's people stand.

features.label: Hearing and seeing again
features.note: As in 5:5-6, John hears one thing (v4) and sees another (v9). The pattern invites readers to interpret one by the other.

features.label: The odd tribal list
features.note: Judah comes first rather than Reuben, the firstborn, perhaps because the Messiah comes from Judah (5:5). Dan, associated with idolatry (Judges 18), is left out.

features.label: Tabernacles imagery
features.note: White robes, palm branches, God's sheltering tent and living water (v9, 15, 17) all recall the Feast of Tabernacles, Israel's festival of joy after harvest.

steps.summary: Revelation 7 answers the terrifying question of who can stand in the day of wrath: those God has sealed and the Lamb has redeemed. Pictured as 144,000 from Israel's tribes and as a countless multitude from all nations, God's people are protected through tribulation and finally stand before his throne, praising him for salvation. The Lamb shepherds them, God shelters them, and every tear is wiped away.

metaArc.book: Chapter 7 is the first interlude in the book, set between the sixth and seventh seals. Its themes of sealing, the 144,000 and the redeemed multitude return in 14:1-5 and in the new Jerusalem of chapters 21-22.
metaArc.redemptive: The chapter fulfills the promise to Abraham of a numberless family from all nations and looks ahead to new creation, where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear (21:3-4).
